copy.title: The Brin Money File
copy.desc: An interactive, fully sourced map of Sergey Brin’s family: Alphabet, 23andMe, the airship company, which stocks you can buy, and the money on the public record.
copy.eyebrow: File #012 · The Brin family · Data as of
copy.h1: Google’s cofounder holds a quarter of the votes. We followed the money.
copy.lede: Who’s who, what each of them built, which companies you can buy stock in, and the money on the public record. Every number links to its source.
copy.familyLede: Tap anyone to open their file. Sergey has three children with two ex-wives. Their names aren’t public, so we only count them.
copy.investLede: Alphabet trades on the Nasdaq as GOOGL and GOOG. 23andMe, which Anne cofounded, is now owned by her nonprofit, and the airship maker LTA is private.
copy.moneyLede: Nearly all of it is Alphabet stock. Sergey owns about 6% of the company but a quarter of its votes, through Class B shares. Only he has a published net worth on this map.
copy.recordLede: What Alphabet’s proxy statement, SEC filings on his gifts and a bankruptcy court show. Filings and reporting, not guesses.
copy.trailLede: From Moscow in 1979 to the fifth-largest fortune on Earth.
copy.calcYearsK: Years to earn what Sergey has
copy.ledgerFoot: Alphabet’s Class B shares carry extra votes, which is how 42.9% of that class adds up to 25.3% of the total vote. “Our sum” means simple addition of the linked filings or reports.

summary.t: Cofounded Google with Larry Page in 1998 while both were Stanford graduate students. He stepped down as president of Alphabet, Google’s parent, in 2019 but stayed on the board as a controlling shareholder, and went back to working on AI in 2023.

owns.t: Cofounder and board member. About 6% of the company and 25.3% of the voting power.

record.t: As of April 6, 2026, he owned 358.9 million Class B shares, 42.9% of that class, giving him 25.3% of Alphabet’s total vote, the 2026 proxy statement shows. Larry Page held 27.4%.

He gave Alphabet shares worth $700 million in May 2025 and more than $1.1 billion in November 2025. Most went to Catalyst4, the nonprofit he started in 2021; the rest to his family foundation and the Michael J. Fox Foundation.

facts.t: His family left the Soviet Union for the U.S. in 1979, when he was 6.
Google’s first office was a Menlo Park garage rented from Susan Wojcicki, his future sister-in-law, for $1,700 a month.
Forbes says he has given more than $2 billion to Parkinson’s research.
He graduated from the University of Maryland at 19.

kidsNote.t: Sergey has three children: two with Anne Wojcicki and one with Nicole Shanahan. Their names aren’t public, so we don’t list them.

summary.t: Cofounded the genetic-testing company 23andMe in 2006 and ran it as CEO until it filed for bankruptcy in 2025. Her nonprofit then bought it back.

worth.none: No current Forbes or Bloomberg estimate.

owns.t: Cofounder. Her nonprofit, TTAM Research Institute, bought nearly all of its assets in 2025.

record.t: 23andMe filed for Chapter 11 in March 2025 and she resigned as CEO. In July a court approved the sale of nearly all its assets to her nonprofit for $305 million, after it outbid Regeneron’s $256 million offer.

facts.t: Her sister Susan ran YouTube from 2014 to 2023.

summary.t: Lawyer and entrepreneur who founded the legal-tech company ClearAccessIP and the Bia-Echo Foundation. She was Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s running mate in his 2024 independent presidential campaign.

facts.t: She sold ClearAccessIP to IPwe in 2020 for about $20 million in stock.
She and Sergey married in 2018 and separated in December 2021; the divorce was final in 2023.

summary.t: Google’s first landlord and its 16th employee. She pushed Google to buy YouTube in 2006 and ran it as CEO from 2014 to 2023. She died in August 2024.

facts.t: She rented her Menlo Park garage to Page and Brin for $1,700 a month in 1998.
Google paid $1.65 billion for YouTube in 2006, a deal she recommended and managed.

summary.t: A retired mathematics professor at the University of Maryland. He moved the family from Moscow to the U.S. in 1979 because of antisemitism in the Soviet Union.
A researcher at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. She died in 2024.
